'Abstract' section.text:
An agent loop without an explicit exit condition spends until an external limit stops it. [2]

This paper names the three exits that vendor documentation supports, and the verification split that decides when the first of them fires. [1][2]

'Introduction' section.text:
An agent loop is a program that calls a model, acts on the reply, and repeats. The repetition is the value and the risk. [2]

A loop with no exit condition spends until an external limit stops it. [2] The limit that arrives is a rate limit or an invoice, neither of which is a design decision.

'Exit conditions' section.text:
A production agent loop stops on a completion signal, a spend cap, or a turn cap. [1][2] Checking them in that order matters. A run that finished and then noticed it was over budget did finish, and reporting that as a cost failure discards completed work.

The Claude Agent SDK exposes the turn cap as `max_turns`. [1] That claim rests on a single source, and no second vendor states it in the same terms.

'Independent verification' section.text:
A checker holding a different tool scope catches errors the maker cannot see in its own output. [3][4] The mechanism is the tool list, not the instruction: a checker with no write tool has no path to edit what it grades.

A checker that shares the maker's context and tools is another self-reflection turn, not independent validation. [4] The split is structural or it is decorative.

'Limitations' section.text:
This paper draws on two runtimes and one paper on self-correction. [4] It measures no loops in production, and it reports no cost figures of its own. [4]

The claim about turn caps rests on a single source. Treat it as documented behavior for one SDK, not as a general property of agent runtimes. [4]
